Coordinate Systems & Map Projections
Representation in GIS
In GIS, representation refers to the methods and techniques used to visualize and communicate spatial 
information. It encompasses various data models, such as vector and raster, and different types of 
geographic features encoded using these models. Representations are crucial for making informed 
decisions about data collection, storage, analysis, and visualization.
The Earth is not a perfect sphere — it is an oblate spheroid, slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at 
the equator. GIS must account for this 3D, irregular shape when representing locations on a flat 2D map.
Why Earth Representation Matters in GIS
Before any map can be made or any coordinate assigned, GIS must answer a fundamental question: how 
do we mathematically model the shape of the Earth so that locations can be precisely defined and 
measured?
The Earth is not a perfect geometric shape — it is irregular, lumpy, and constantly changing. GIS solves 
this by using a series of increasingly simplified models, each serving a different purpose, moving from the 
complex real shape to a workable mathematical approximation.
The Three Models of Earth's Shape
1. The Geoid — The True Physical Shape

The Three Models of Earth's Shape
1. The Geoid — The True Physical Shape
The geoid is the actual, irregular shape of the Earth as defined by gravity. It represents the surface 
where gravitational pull is equal everywhere — roughly corresponding to mean sea level extended across 
the entire planet, including through continents.
Key characteristics:

Lumpy and irregular — gravity varies from place to place due to differences in rock density, 
topography, and internal structure

Bulges where mass is concentrated (mountain ranges, dense rock) and dips where mass is lower 
(ocean trenches)

Cannot be described by a simple mathematical equation

Why it matters: When you say a mountain is 1,000 meters high, that height is measured relative to the 
geoid — mean sea level — not a geometric shape.
Why we don't use it for coordinates: It is too mathematically complex to use as the basis for a 
coordinate system. You cannot write a formula for it.
2. The Ellipsoid — The Mathematical Model
Because the geoid is too irregular for mathematical calculation, GIS uses an ellipsoid — a smooth, 
mathematically defined shape that closely approximates the Earth's true form.
An ellipsoid is essentially a sphere that has been slightly squashed at the poles and bulged at the 
equator — reflecting the fact that the Earth's rotation causes it to be wider than it is tall.
Defined by two parameters:

Semi-major axis (a) — the radius at the Equator (approximately 6,378 km)

Semi-minor axis (b) — the radius at the poles (approximately 6,357 km)

Flattening (f) — describes how much the ellipsoid deviates from a perfect sphere: f = (a − b) ÷ a ≈ 
1/298.257
Why it matters: The ellipsoid provides the smooth, calculable surface on which latitude and longitude are 
mathematically defined.

Local Datums
Designed to fit the ellipsoid as precisely as possible to a specific region — accepting a poorer fit

The ellipsoid is offset from the Earth's centre to better match the geoid in a particular area.





The problem with local datums: A location may have noticeably different coordinates under a local 
datum compared to WGS84 — differences can range from a few centimetres to several hundred metres 
depending on the region.

From 3D Earth to 2D Map — The Projection Step

Once the Earth's shape is modelled using an ellipsoid and a datum, GIS faces one final challenge: how to 
represent this curved 3D surface on a flat 2D screen or paper map.
This is the role of map projection — a mathematical transformation that converts 3D spherical coordinates 
(latitude, longitude) into 2D flat coordinates (x, y in metres).
The relationship between the three models and the map works as a pipeline:

Mathematical model (Ellipsoid)
       ↓
Anchored to Earth (Datum)
       ↓
Projected to flat surface (Map Projection)
       ↓
2D Map with x, y coordinates

What is a Geographic Coordinate System (GCS)?
A Geographic Coordinate System is a reference framework that uses a three-dimensional spherical 
surface to define locations anywhere on the Earth. Instead of measuring in metres or feet, it measures 
positions using angles expressed in degrees — telling you how far north or south and how far east or west 
a location is from fixed reference lines.

It is the most fundamental way of expressing location on Earth and forms the basis of all GPS technology, 
global datasets, and satellite navigation systems.
The Two Core Measurements
Latitude (φ)
Latitude measures north–south position relative to the Equator.

The Equator is 0° latitude — the reference line dividing the northern and southern hemispheres

The North Pole is 90° North (90°N)

The South Pole is 90° South (90°S)

Lines of equal latitude run horizontally around the Earth and are called parallels — they are always 
parallel to each other and never intersect

Every location on Earth has a unique latitude value between 90°S and 90°N
What latitude tells you: how close a location is to the Equator or the poles — and by extension, its 
general climate zone.
Longitude (λ)
Longitude measures east–west position relative to the Prime Meridian.

The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich, England and is defined as 0° longitude

Longitude ranges from 0° to 180° East and 0° to 180° West


How Coordinates Are Written
A location is expressed as a coordinate pair (latitude, longitude). There are two common notation 
formats:

Degrees-Minutes-Seconds (DMS) The traditional format, breaking each degree into 60 minutes and each 
minute into 60 seconds:
Freetown, Sierra Leone: 8° 27' 57" N, 13° 13' 54" W
Decimal Degrees (DD) The modern digital format used in GIS software and GPS devices — minutes and 
seconds are converted into a decimal fraction of a degree:
Freetown, Sierra Leone: 8.4658° N, 13.2317° W
Decimal degrees are the standard in GIS because they are easier to store, process, and calculate with 
computationally.
Converting DMS to DD:
DD = Degrees + (Minutes ÷ 60) + (Seconds ÷ 3600)

The Graticule
The network of parallels and meridians drawn across a globe or map is called the graticule. It forms the 
grid system of the GCS — every intersection of a parallel and a meridian uniquely identifies one location on 
Earth.
Units of Measurement
GCS coordinates are measured in angular units — degrees (°). This is important because it means:

You cannot directly calculate distances in metres from GCS coordinates without additional 
mathematics


A degree of latitude is always approximately 111 kilometres regardless of where you are on Earth

A degree of longitude varies in distance depending on latitude — at the Equator it is ~111km, but 
it shrinks to 0km at the poles where all meridians converge
This is why GCS is not suitable for direct distance or area measurement — and why a Projected 
Coordinate System is needed for analysis.
Relationship to Datum and Ellipsoid
A GCS is not just the latitude/longitude grid — it is built on three components working together:
Ellipsoid — the mathematical model of the Earth's shape (slightly flattened sphere) on which the 
coordinate measurements are based.
Datum — defines how the ellipsoid is positioned and oriented relative to the real Earth.

Limitations of GCS

Cannot measure in linear units — degrees are angular, not metric. You cannot calculate area in 
hectares or distance in kilometres directly from GCS coordinates.

Longitude spacing varies — one degree of longitude near the poles is far shorter on the ground 
than one degree near the Equator, making GCS unsuitable for consistent spatial analysis.

Not suitable for local precision — for detailed, local-scale analysis (land surveys, urban planning, 
infrastructure mapping), a Projected Coordinate System is always preferred.
What is a Projected Coordinate System (PCS)?
A Projected Coordinate System is a mathematical transformation that converts the curved, three-
dimensional surface of the Earth into a flat, two-dimensional plane — making it possible to display the 
world on a screen, paper map, or any flat surface.
While a Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) tells you where something is using angles (degrees of 
latitude and longitude), a PCS tells you exactly how far things are from each other using linear units — 
metres or feet. This makes measurement, analysis, and mapping practical and accurate.

Why Projection is Necessary

The Earth is a three-dimensional sphere. Maps, screens, and paper are two-dimensional. This creates a 
fundamental geometric problem — you cannot flatten a curved surface without distorting it, just as you 
cannot flatten an orange peel without tearing or stretching it.
Projection solves this by applying a mathematical formula that systematically converts spherical 
latitude/longitude coordinates into flat x, y coordinates — accepting some distortion as an unavoidable 
trade-off in exchange for a workable flat surface.
How a PCS Works
A PCS is built on three components working together:
1. A Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) The PCS starts with a GCS — the datum and ellipsoid that 
define the Earth's shape and the origin of coordinates. The GCS provides the 3D surface that will be 
projected.
2. A Projection Method The mathematical formula used to transform spherical coordinates into flat 
coordinates. Different projection methods produce different results and different patterns of distortion.
3. Projection Parameters Settings that control how the projection is applied — including the central 
meridian, standard parallels, false easting, and false northing.

ifferent patterns of distortion.
3. Projection Parameters Settings that control how the projection is applied — including the central 
meridian, standard parallels, false easting, and false northing. These parameters fine-tune the projection to 
minimise distortion for a specific region.
Coordinate Units in a PCS
Unlike GCS which uses degrees, a PCS expresses all coordinates in linear units:

Easting (X) — the horizontal distance east or west from a central reference line, measured in 
metres

Northing (Y) — the vertical distance north or south from a reference point, measured in metres
False Easting and False Northing To avoid negative coordinate values (which complicate calculations), 
most PCS systems add a large constant to the easting and northing values — shifting the origin so all 
coordinates within the zone are positive.
For example, in UTM: a false easting of 500,000 metres is added so the central meridian of each zone 
always has an easting of 500,000m, and all values to its left and right remain positive.

Web Mercator (EPSG: 3857)
The projection used by Google Maps, OpenStreetMap, Bing Maps, and virtually every web mapping 
platform.
Key characteristics:

Based on the Mercator projection applied to a sphere rather than an ellipsoid


Coordinates expressed in metres but referenced to the Equator and Prime Meridian
Why it is used for web maps: The Mercator projection produces a rectangular map where north is always

Important: Web Mercator should never be used for area or distance analysis — its distortions make

A conic projection that preserves area accurately across large regions.
Key characteristics:



A conic projection that preserves shape (conformal) across mid-latitude regions.


Area is distorted away from the standard parallels
Best used for: Aeronautical charts, meteorological maps, and regional topographic mapping in mid-
latitude countries.

The Reprojection Process
When you have data in GCS (degrees) and need to analyse it in a PCS (metres), GIS software performs a 
reprojection — mathematically transforming every coordinate in the dataset from the source CRS to the 
target CRS.
This process involves:
1.Reading each coordinate pair (latitude, longitude) from the source GCS
2.Applying the datum transformation if the source and target use different datums
3.Applying the projection formula to convert angular coordinates to linear x, y values

4.Writing the new coordinates in the target PCS
Modern GIS software (QGIS, ArcGIS) handles this automatically — but the analyst must always specify 
the correct source and target CRS to ensure the transformation is accurate.
Types of Map Projections
Map projections are classified by the geometric surface used to unwrap the Earth from a sphere onto a 
flat plane. Imagine placing a light source inside a transparent globe and projecting its features onto a 
surrounding surface — the shape of that surface determines the projection type.
Cylindrical Projections
A cylinder is wrapped around the Earth, touching it along a great circle (usually the Equator).

surrounding surface — the shape of that surface determines the projection type.
Cylindrical Projections
A cylinder is wrapped around the Earth, touching it along a great circle (usually the Equator). The Earth's 
features are projected onto the cylinder, which is then unrolled into a flat rectangle.
Characteristics:

Most accurate along the line of tangency (usually the Equator)

Distortion increases progressively toward the poles

Produces a rectangular map where lines of latitude and longitude form a perfect grid
Variants:

Normal cylindrical — cylinder wraps around the Equator (standard orientation)

Transverse cylindrical — cylinder is rotated 90° to touch along a meridian (used in UTM)

Oblique cylindrical — cylinder touches along any other great circle
Common examples:
Mercator Projection — the most famous cylindrical projection, developed in 1569 for navigation. Preserves 
shape and angles (conformal) — a straight line on a Mercator map represents a constant compass 
bearing, making it ideal for navigation. However, it severely exaggerates the size of landmasses near the 
poles. Greenland appears as large as Africa, despite Africa being 14 times larger.
Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) — uses a transverse cylinder touching along a meridian. Divides the 
Earth into 60 narrow zones, each 6° wide, providing high accuracy within each zone.

Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) — uses a transverse cylinder touching along a meridian. Divides the 
Earth into 60 narrow zones, each 6° wide, providing high accuracy within each zone. The standard 
projection for local and regional GIS work worldwide.
Web Mercator (EPSG: 3857) — a simplified version of Mercator used by Google Maps, OpenStreetMap, 
and all major web mapping platforms. Convenient for display but unsuitable for measurement.
Best for: Equatorial regions, navigation, web mapping, and any application where direction must be 
preserved.

Conical Projections
A cone is placed over the Earth, touching it along one or two lines of latitude called standard parallels. 
Features are projected onto the cone, which is then unrolled flat.
Characteristics:

Most accurate along the standard parallels where the cone touches the Earth

Distortion increases away from the standard parallels — least toward the poles, most toward the 
Equator

Best suited for mid-latitude regions with greater east-west than north-south extent
Common examples:
Albers Equal-Area Conic — uses two standard parallels and preserves area accurately across the entire 
map. A region twice as large on the ground appears twice as large on the map. Shape is slightly distorted 
but area relationships are always correct. Standard projection for US national maps and continental-scale 
analysis.
Lambert Conformal Conic — preserves shape (conformal) near the standard parallels.

but area relationships are always correct. Standard projection for US national maps and continental-scale 
analysis.
Lambert Conformal Conic — preserves shape (conformal) near the standard parallels. Angles and local 
forms are accurate — a circular lake appears circular. Used for aeronautical charts, weather maps, and 
mid-latitude topographic mapping.
Best for: Mid-latitude countries and continents, area comparison, regional topographic and meteorological 
mapping.
Planar (Azimuthal) Projections
A flat plane touches the Earth at a single point — usually the North or South Pole, but can be any point on 
the surface. Features are projected outward from that point of tangency onto the plane.
Characteristics:

Most accurate at the central point of tangency

Distortion increases radially outward from the centre

Preserves true direction (azimuth) from the centre point to any other point — a straight line from 
the centre represents a true compass bearing
Common examples:
Stereographic — a conformal azimuthal projection used for polar regions and large-scale mapping. 
Preserves shape near the centre. Used as the standard projection for Antarctic and Arctic mapping.
Orthographic — projects the Earth as it would appear from infinite distance in space. Produces the familiar 
"globe view" appearance — realistic but highly distorted at the edges.

Azimuthal Equidistant — preserves true distances from the centre point to all other points. Used in aviation 
and long-distance communication planning. Famously used in the United Nations emblem.
Best for: Polar regions, aviation route planning, and any analysis requiring true direction from a central

Projection Distortions
Every map projection distorts the Earth's surface in some way — this is mathematically unavoidable. When 
a curved surface is flattened, something must stretch, compress, or shift. There are four spatial properties 
that can be distorted, and no single projection can preserve all four simultaneously.
The Four Types of Distortion
1. Area Distortion The size of features on the map does not match their true size on the Earth.
The most notorious example is the Mercator projection — Greenland appears roughly the same size as 
Africa on a Mercator map, but Africa is actually approximately 14 times larger.

size on the Earth.
The most notorious example is the Mercator projection — Greenland appears roughly the same size as 
Africa on a Mercator map, but Africa is actually approximately 14 times larger. This is because the 
Mercator projection stretches features increasingly toward the poles to maintain shape, causing extreme 
area exaggeration at high latitudes.
Projections that eliminate area distortion are called equal-area (equivalent) projections. On these maps, 
if a country occupies 2% of the map's area, it occupies 2% of the Earth's surface. Shape is sacrificed to 
achieve this.
Examples of equal-area projections: Albers Equal-Area Conic, Sinusoidal, Mollweide, Goode's Homolosine.
When it matters: Any analysis involving comparing sizes — population density mapping, land cover 
statistics, agricultural area calculations, environmental assessments.
2. Shape Distortion (Conformality) The shape of features on the map does not match their true shape on 
the Earth.
Shape distortion manifests as stretching or compression in specific directions — a circular island may 
appear elongated or squashed depending on its position on the map and the projection used.

rth.
Shape distortion manifests as stretching or compression in specific directions — a circular island may 
appear elongated or squashed depending on its position on the map and the projection used.

Projections that eliminate shape distortion are called conformal projections. They preserve angles and 
local shapes — if two roads meet at a 45° angle on the ground, they meet at 45° on the map. However, 
preserving shape requires sacrificing area accuracy.
Examples of conformal projections: Mercator, Lambert Conformal Conic, Stereographic.
When it matters: Navigation, weather mapping, topographic mapping, and any application where the shape 
of features must appear natural and undistorted.
3. Distance Distortion Measured distances on the map do not reflect true distances on the Earth.
Except at specific lines or points, most projections stretch or compress distances unevenly across the map. 
A ruler measurement between two cities will give different results depending on where those cities sit 
relative to the projection's zone of accuracy.
Projections that eliminate distance distortion along specific lines are called equidistant projections.

relative to the projection's zone of accuracy.
Projections that eliminate distance distortion along specific lines are called equidistant projections. They 
preserve true distances from one point (or along specific lines) to all other points — but cannot preserve 
distances everywhere simultaneously.
Examples of equidistant projections: Azimuthal Equidistant, Equidistant Conic, Plate Carrée.
When it matters: Measuring routes between locations, proximity analysis, calculating travel distances, and 
communication network planning.
4. Direction Distortion (Azimuth) Compass bearings and angular relationships between features are 
misrepresented on the map.
On a distorted map, a straight line between two points does not represent a true compass bearing — an 
aircraft flying a straight line on the map would actually be following a curved path on the Earth.
Projections that eliminate direction distortion from a central point are called azimuthal projections.

The Fundamental Rule — The Projection Dilemma
A projection can preserve area or shape — never both.
This is not a technical limitation that better mathematics can solve — it is a geometric truth proven by Carl 
Friedrich Gauss in the 19th century. The theorem states that a curved surface cannot be flattened without 
distortion of at least one spatial property.
Every projection represents a deliberate choice about which distortion to accept:

Compromise projections like the Robinson and Winkel Tripel do not perfectly preserve any single 
property — instead they distribute distortion evenly across the map to produce a visually balanced result. 
These are popular for world maps in atlases and educational materials.
Tissot's Indicatrix — Visualising Distortion
Cartographers use a tool called Tissot's Indicatrix to visualise projection distortion. Small circles of equal 
size are placed at regular intervals across a globe. When the projection is applied, these circles deform — 
stretching into ellipses where there is distortion. The shape and size of the ellipses reveal exactly where 
and how much each projection distorts area, shape, distance, and direction.

Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)
A Coordinate Reference System is the complete, formal framework that defines exactly how coordinates 
relate to real locations on the Earth's surface. It is not just a projection or just a datum — it is the full 
package of all the information needed to unambiguously interpret a coordinate pair.
What a CRS Contains
A complete CRS specification includes:
Datum — defines the ellipsoid and how it is anchored to the Earth, establishing the origin and orientation of 
the coordinate system.
Ellipsoid — the mathematical model of the Earth's shape on which coordinates are calculated.
Projection — the mathematical method used to transform 3D spherical coordinates into 2D flat 
coordinates (for projected CRS only).
Projection parameters — the specific settings applied to the projection: central meridian, standard 
parallels, false easting, false northing, scale factor.
Unit of measurement — degrees for geographic CRS, metres or feet for projected CRS.

Without all of these components being defined and consistent, coordinates cannot be accurately 
interpreted or compared between datasets.
Two Categories of CRS
Geographic CRS (GCRS) Based on a 3D spherical surface. Coordinates expressed in degrees of latitude 
and longitude. Used for global data storage, GPS, and as the foundation for projected CRS.
Example: WGS84 (EPSG: 4326) — the global standard.
Projected CRS (PCRS) Based on a flat 2D plane. Coordinates expressed in linear units (metres). Used for 
local and regional mapping, measurement, and spatial analysis.
Example: UTM Zone 29N (EPSG: 32629) — appropriate for Sierra Leone.
EPSG Codes — The Universal CRS Identifier
Every recognised CRS is assigned a unique numerical code by the EPSG (European Petroleum Survey 
Group) registry — now maintained by the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers (IOGP).
EPSG codes provide a universal shorthand — instead of describing an entire CRS in words, a single 
number uniquely identifies it.

Datum Concepts — WGS84
What is a Datum?
A datum is a reference framework that anchors the mathematical ellipsoid to the real, physical 
Earth. It defines:

Which ellipsoid model is used

Where the ellipsoid is positioned relative to the Earth's centre of mass

The orientation of the coordinate axes

The point or surface from which all measurements originate
Without a datum, coordinates are mathematically valid but physically meaningless — like giving directions 
without specifying the starting point.
Why Different Datums Exist
Historically, different countries and regions developed their own local datums, each designed to fit the 
ellipsoid as precisely as possible to their specific part of the Earth's surface.

Historically, different countries and regions developed their own local datums, each designed to fit the

With the advent of GPS and satellite geodesy, global datums were developed to provide a single consistent 
reference for the entire Earth — essential for navigation, international data sharing, and global GIS.
WGS84 — The Global Standard
WGS84 (World Geodetic System 1984) is the most important datum in modern GIS and the foundation of 
the global GPS system.

NAD27 (North American Datum 1927) An older local datum using the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid, centred on 
Meades Ranch, Kansas. Differences from WGS84 can reach up to 100 metres in some locations. Many 
historical US maps and datasets use NAD27 — reprojection to WGS84 or NAD83 is essential before 
mixing with modern data.
ED50 (European Datum 1950) The post-World War II standard for European mapping. Differences from 
WGS84 range from 50 to 200 metres across Europe. Largely replaced by ETRS89, which is aligned to 
WGS84.
Local African Datums Many African countries have historical local datums from colonial-era surveys. 
Sierra Leone and much of West Africa historically used datums tied to older triangulation surveys. Modern 
GIS work in the region uses WGS84 or the UTM Zone 29N projected CRS built on it.
Datum Shifts — Why They Matter
Because different datums position the ellipsoid differently relative to the Earth, the same physical 
location will have different coordinates in different datums. This is called a datum shift.

Practical consequence: If you overlay a dataset in WGS84 with a dataset in an older local datum without 
performing a datum transformation, features that should perfectly align — like a road and its land parcels 
— will be offset by the datum shift distance. In urban mapping or infrastructure work, this can cause serious 
errors.
Datum transformation is the mathematical process of converting coordinates from one datum to another. 
GIS software performs this automatically if both datums are correctly specified — but only if the analyst has 
correctly identified and set the CRS of each dataset.

Importance of CRS in Analysis
The Core Principle
CRS is not a background technical setting — it is the foundation on which every GIS measurement, 
overlay, and analytical result is built. If the CRS is wrong, mismatched, or undefined, every output from 
the analysis is unreliable regardless of how sophisticated the analysis itself is.
The principle is straightforward: all layers in a GIS analysis must share a consistent, appropriate CRS 
— or results will be spatially incorrect.
Why CRS Matters in Practice
1. Spatial Alignment and Overlay Accuracy The most immediate consequence of a CRS mismatch is 
that layers do not align. A road network stored in WGS84 and a parcel boundary layer stored in a local 
datum will be offset when overlaid — sometimes by tens or hundreds of metres.
This misalignment means that spatial queries produce wrong results — a point that should fall inside a 
polygon falls outside it, a road that should intersect a watershed boundary misses it, a building that should 
overlap a flood zone does not.
In GIS, garbage CRS in = garbage results out, regardless of data quality.
2. Accurate Distance Measurement Distances calculated in a Geographic CRS (degrees) are not in 
metres — they are in degrees of arc, which represent different physical distances at different latitudes.
One degree of longitude at the Equator ≈ 111 kilometres. One degree of longitude at 60° North ≈ 55 
kilometres — half the distance.

One degree of longitude at the Equator ≈ 111 kilometres. One degree of longitude at 60° North ≈ 55 
kilometres — half the distance. Calculating the distance between two points in degrees and treating the 
result as kilometres introduces serious error, especially at higher latitudes.

Rule: Always reproject data to an appropriate projected CRS (such as UTM) before calculating distances. 
Distances should always be expressed in metres, not degrees.
3. Accurate Area Calculation Area calculations in a Geographic CRS are equally unreliable. A polygon's 
area calculated in square degrees is meaningless as a physical measurement — square degrees are not a 
unit of area.
Furthermore, if data is in a projected CRS but the wrong one is chosen — for example, using a projection 
optimised for North America to analyse land in West Africa — area calculations will be distorted by the 
projection's inherent inaccuracies at that location.
Rule: Always use an equal-area projection appropriate for the study region when calculating areas in 
hectares, square kilometres, or any other real-world unit.
4. Geoprocessing and Spatial Operations Every geoprocessing operation in GIS — buffering, clipping, 
intersecting, merging, dissolving — assumes that input layers share a common CRS.

4. Geoprocessing and Spatial Operations Every geoprocessing operation in GIS — buffering, clipping, 
intersecting, merging, dissolving — assumes that input layers share a common CRS. When they do not, 
results are geometrically incorrect.
A 500-metre buffer drawn in a Geographic CRS will not be 500 metres on the ground — it will be 500 units 
of degrees, which is geographically meaningless. In a Projected CRS (metres), a 500-metre buffer is 
precisely 500 metres in every direction.
5. Remote Sensing and Raster Analysis When combining vector and raster data — for example, 
extracting land cover values at survey point locations, or masking a satellite image with an administrative 
boundary — both datasets must share the same CRS. Mismatched CRS causes the extraction to sample 
the wrong locations, producing entirely incorrect results.
6. Data Integration from Multiple Sources Real GIS projects almost always combine data from multiple 
sources — government agencies, satellite providers, field surveys, online databases. Each source may use 
a different CRS. Before any analysis begins, all datasets must be identified, checked, and if necessary 
reprojected into a single common CRS.
Failing to do this is one of the most common sources of error in GIS projects, particularly for beginners.

The international standard for data sharing is WGS84 (EPSG: 4326) for geographic data, which ensures 
universal compatibility across all GIS platforms.

On-the-Fly Projection — A Common Misunderstanding
Most GIS software can display layers with different CRS together by temporarily reprojecting them on 
screen — this is called on-the-fly projection. It makes layers appear to align visually, which can create a 
false sense of security.
On-the-fly projection does not fix the underlying CRS mismatch for analysis. It only adjusts the 
display. All calculations, measurements, and geoprocessing still operate on the original coordinates — so if 
the CRS is mismatched, analytical results will still be wrong even if the map looks correct.
Best Practices for CRS Management
Set the project CRS first — before adding any data, define the CRS for the entire project. All subsequent 
data should be reprojected to match.
Always verify the CRS of incoming data — never assume a dataset's CRS. Check it explicitly before 
adding it to a project.
Reproject, do not just reassign — reassigning a CRS (telling the software "this is now UTM") without 
reprojecting is wrong. Reprojection mathematically transforms the coordinates.

Use equal-area projections for area analysis — for area calculations, always choose a projection that
